description: We are a team of developers and researchers participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We analyze 3D structures using SPHEREx data and apply machine learning to search for signatures of Planet X. Our goal is to transform open NASA data into accurate mathematical models, robust algorithms, and web services.
summary:
I developed an automated Python pipeline for querying, calibrating, and inspecting astronomical imaging data from NASA’s SPHEREx Data Release 1 archive via the IPAC IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA) service.

Raw space-telescope exposures contain substantial foreground zodiacal light and detector artifacts, while downloading full-frame FITS files for multi-epoch sky targets creates heavy bandwidth overhead. This pipeline solves these challenges by programmatically querying observations by sky coordinates and detector band, subsampling time-series frames, and requesting targeted server-side FITS cutouts. It then isolates true astrophysical emission by subtracting the built-in zodiacal background model, applies a custom bitwise quality-flag mask to exclude corrupted pixels, generates side-by-side diagnostic visualizations with World Coordinate System (WCS) projections, and constructs a standardized tangent-plane target WCS grid for downstream image co-addition.

This tool is significant because it streamlines multi-epoch data reduction for SPHEREx’s all-sky spectrophotometric survey. By automating background removal, quality filtering, and astrometric grid preparation, it enables researchers to rapidly inspect transient sources, verify data integrity, and prepare clean datasets for deeper astronomical analysis.
details:
Project Details: SPHEREx Data Reduction & Inspection Pipeline

What does it do and how does it work? This project is an automated astronomical data-processing pipeline built to query, calibrate, and visualize near-infrared sky observations from NASA’s SPHEREx Data Release 1 archive. The workflow operates in five distinct stages:

  1. Archive Querying & Temporal Sampling: Using target sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) and a specified detector bandpass (e.g., SPHEREx-D6), the pipeline queries the IPAC IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA) service, sorts observations chronologically by Modified Julian Date (t_min), and uniformly subsamples large multi-epoch datasets.
  2. Server-Side Cutout Generation: Instead of downloading massive full-detector FITS files, it dynamically constructs HTTP cutout URLs tailored to a specific field of view (fov), drastically reducing data transfer overhead.
  3. Background Subtraction & Bitwise Masking: Upon loading the multi-extension FITS data (IMAGE, ZODI, FLAGS), the script subtracts the zodiacal light foreground model (IMAGE - ZODI) and applies a custom 32-bit integer bitmask (bad_bits) to isolate and replace corrupted or saturated pixels with NaN values.
  4. Astrometric Grid Alignment: It extracts native World Coordinate System (WCS) metadata, calculates average pixel scales, and generates a standardized square tangent-plane (RA---TAN, DEC--TAN) target WCS grid centered on the object for downstream image co-addition or time-series blinking.
  5. Diagnostic Visualization: Finally, it renders a three-panel WCS-projected plot displaying the raw science exposure, the background-subtracted/masked residual, and the binary bad-pixel mask using AsinhStretch normalization to preserve both faint nebular details and bright point sources.

What advantages does it have?

  • Bandwidth and Storage Efficiency: Server-side spatial cutouts combined with intelligent temporal subsampling allow rapid inspection of multi-epoch targets without saturating local disk space or network bandwidth.
  • Automated Quality Control: Bitwise flag filtering eliminates manual inspection of telemetry headers, ensuring detector anomalies do not contaminate photometric or visual analysis.
  • Astrometric Readiness: By constructing a standardized tangent-plane target WCS directly from native detector pixel scales, the pipeline prepares heterogeneous exposures for immediate alignment, stacking, or blink comparison.

What are the anticipated impacts of the project? As SPHEREx conducts its all-sky spectrophotometric survey, astronomers face the challenge of sifting through millions of spectral images to detect transient phenomena, variable stars, and faint solar system bodies. This tool lowers the technical barrier to working with SPHEREx Data Release 1 products. It accelerates the initial data-triage phase for researchers, citizen scientists, and students, enabling faster discovery of time-domain events and cleaner inputs for scientific pipelines.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Language: Python 3.
  • Core Scientific Libraries: Astropy (for FITS file handling, sky coordinates, WCS transformations, unit management, and AsinhStretch image normalization), Astroquery (specifically astroquery.ipac.irsa for querying NASA/IPAC archives), NumPy (for array mathematics and bitwise flag operations), and Matplotlib (for WCS-projected multi-panel data visualization).
  • Data Standards & Services: FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) multi-extension data format and the IPAC IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA) web protocol.
  • Development Environment & Hardware: Developed on a standard Windows workstation using Visual Studio Code / PyCharm, demonstrating that space-telescope data reduction can be executed locally without specialized supercomputing hardware.

How creative is your project? Rather than treating astronomical images as static pictures, the project creatively combines network-level optimization with low-level bitwise telemetry manipulation. Constructing a custom integer bitmask via bit-shifting (1 << bit) to filter specific hardware artifacts while dynamically building a standardized TAN-projection target grid bridges the gap between raw archive access and publication-ready astrometric alignment in a lightweight, modular script.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Server & Network Reliability: Because querying external archives can trigger gateway timeouts (such as HTTP 502 proxy errors on the IPAC/Caltech gateway), the pipeline was designed around lightweight cutout URLs and capped frame counts (max_frames) to minimize server strain.
  • Dynamic Range of Astronomical Data: Raw infrared images span several orders of magnitude in brightness; linear scaling hides faint structures, so we implemented percentile clipping (99.5%) paired with inverse hyperbolic sine (AsinhStretch) scaling.
  • Edge-Case Resilience: When a frame is heavily corrupted or entirely masked out, standard normalization fails. We built defensive checks (np.any(np.isfinite(...))) to flag problematic frames gracefully without crashing batch processing runs.
  • Coordinate Precision: Preserving sub-arcsecond astrometric accuracy when transitioning from native detector coordinates to a custom tangent-plane grid required exact calculation of proj_plane_pixel_scales and half-pixel center offsets ((n + 1) / 2).
